keyTerms.definition: y^{(i)}(w^T x^{(i)} + b), the signed score.
The functional margin divided by ||w||: the Euclidean distance to the boundary.
Rescaling (w, b) leaves geometric margins fixed.

recall.question: What is the difference between functional and geometric margin?
recall.answer: Functional: the signed score y(w^T x + b); scaling (w, b) doubles it without changing predictions. Geometric: functional divided by ||w||, the actual Euclidean distance, immune to scale.

recall.question: In the computed example, what are the two margins?
recall.answer: w = [3,4], b = -25, x = (4,3), y = 1: score -1, functional margin -1, ||w|| = 5, geometric margin -0.2. Scaled by 2: functional -2, geometric still -0.2.

recall.question: Why not maximize the functional margin directly?
recall.answer: The optimizer scales (w, b) to infinity instead of moving the boundary.

keyTerms.definition: The (w, b) optimization: min (1/2)||w||^2 with margin constraints.
Strict separation with a maximized gap.
The problem is unchanged by rescaling (w, b).

recall.question: What is the hard-margin primal?
recall.answer: min_{w,b} (1/2)||w||^2 subject to y^{(i)}(w^T x^{(i)} + b) >= 1 for all i.

recall.question: Why fix the functional margin to 1?
recall.answer: The problem is scale-invariant. With ||w|| = 1 non-convex, rescaling fixes the functional margin to 1, so gamma = 1/||w|| and maximizing gamma equals minimizing (1/2)||w||^2.

recall.question: What happens on non-separable data?
recall.answer: No (w, b) satisfies all constraints. The primal is infeasible.

keyTerms.definition: W(alpha) depending only on inner products, with alpha_i >= 0.
Stationarity, primal and dual feasibility, complementary slackness.

recall.question: What are the KKT conditions?
recall.answer: Stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementary slackness: alpha_i [y^{(i)}(w^T x^{(i)} + b) - 1] = 0.

recall.question: Why does the dual matter?
recall.answer: Two wins: the data enters only through inner products, so kernels slot in; the solution is sparse, most alpha_i = 0.

recall.question: Why does SMO update pairs, not single alphas?
recall.answer: The sum alpha_i y^{(i)} = 0 constraint pins a single alpha given the rest, so one-at-a-time ascent cannot move.

keyTerms.definition: An example with alpha_i > 0, sitting on the margin.
The per-example constraint price; nonzero only on support vectors.

recall.question: What is a support vector?
recall.answer: An example with alpha_i > 0, sitting exactly on the margin (or violating it, soft case). All other examples have alpha_i = 0 and do not affect w or predictions.

recall.question: Are support vectors the misclassified points?
recall.answer: No: they are the margin points. A separable dataset has zero errors and still has support vectors.

sections.title: SL-05: Soft margins and the C parameter

keyTerms.definition: xi_i, the margin violation in functional units, priced at C per unit.
Margin with violations allowed at a price.
0 <= alpha_i <= C: the only dual change for the soft margin.

recall.question: What does large versus small C do?
recall.answer: Large C: violations are expensive, the boundary bends to outliers (hard-margin behavior). Small C: violations are cheap, the margin stays wide and some examples fall inside or across.

recall.question: What changes in the dual for the soft margin?
recall.answer: Only the box changes: 0 <= alpha_i <= C. Everything else is the same W(alpha).

recall.question: Why pick C by cross-validation, not test accuracy?
recall.answer: C picked by test accuracy spends the test set. Pick C by cross-validation.

keyTerms.definition: Optimizing one alpha at a time; blocked by the sum constraint.
Sequential minimal optimization: analytic pair updates clipped to [L, H].
Clipping the pair update to the box segment [L, H].

recall.question: Why must SMO update pairs?
recall.answer: The sum alpha_i y^{(i)} = 0 constraint pins a single alpha given the rest. Two at a time: the constraint becomes a line, the box clips to [L, H], the 1-D quadratic has a closed-form max.

recall.question: What does each pair update cost?
recall.answer: O(1) given cached errors. A full pass is O(n^2) kernel evals naive, O(n) with caching.

keyTerms.definition: Whether the features admit a separating boundary.
Test data follows the same geometry as training.

recall.question: What does an infeasible hard-margin fit diagnose?
recall.answer: The data is not separable in the current features. Options: add slack (C), change the kernel, add features.

recall.question: Why is separability not sufficient?
recall.answer: A kernel that separates training perfectly with tiny sigma destroys generalization. Separability is necessary, not sufficient.
